title: Robert White Could be Ineligible for Election Unless He Resigns
text:
Robert White Could be Ineligible for Election Unless He Resigns · City Cast DC CITY CAST DC Podcasts

 Become a Neighbor CITY CAST DC Politics News Business Cops & Courts Culture Food & Drink D.C. Guides D.C., Explained Opinion Politics Robert White Could be Ineligible for Election Unless He Resigns 
 An obscure legal provision bans current officeholders from becoming the D.C. delegate. Now White wants to change the law.
 Ben Brasch and Michael Schaffer Oct 27, 2026 · 11:12 a.m. ET D.C. Councilmember Robert White. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images) Democratic nominee Robert White could be ineligible for election as the District’s congressional delegate unless he resigns his D.C. Council seat before Election Day, thanks to an obscure provision of the 1970 law that established the position. The law says the delegate must not hold another paid public office on Election Day. 
 Now White, who only belatedly became aware of the provision, is looking into hurriedly changing the law, according to three councilmembers who have been in touch with White or his staff about it. The councilmembers spoke anonymously because of sensitive matters concerning their colleague.
 Without the change, White would need to leave his Council job by Tuesday, forgoing two months of salary before he would presumably take office in January. White, who is serving his third term as an at-large member of the D.C. Council and currently chairs the housing committee, makes $171,547 a year.
 White did not respond to requests for comment. A member of White’s campaign told City Cast DC that they are researching the issue and looking into the best next steps.
 The Washington Sun reported that White disputed not knowing about the provision until recently: “This isn’t new to me. We’ve had a legal theory on this for quite some time.” He added: “I’ve got a few days to make a call and determination, but I’m not going to jeopardize going into Congress.”
 In internal communications reviewed by City Cast DC, White’s staff told councilmembers that they have asked the Council’s legal office to study whether local lawmakers even have the power to change the law, which appears in both the D.C. code and the U.S. code.
 Assuming the answer is yes, it still won’t be easy. The D.C. Council is not slated to meet this week, so they’d need to gather for a special meeting and pass so-called emergency legislation, which requires a supermajority.
 Any bill would also need to be signed into law by Mayor Muriel Bowser, a past political rival of White’s.
 Many inside the Wilson Building are confused as to how White could have missed this provision of the code and how this is going to play out. They’re also unsure why White wouldn’t just resign from an office he’s planning to leave anyway — instead of pondering a complicated process to change the law and permit himself two more lame-duck months.
 “This is a tricky juncture and, at the moment nobody knows where it’s going to land,” said one of the councilmembers.
 Even if White managed to convene an emergency D.C. Council meeting before the election, it’s not clear he has the votes. And even if he is able to pass the bill, the mayor would need to sign it by Election Day. Legally, she has 10 days to approve it — a potential issue because White doesn’t have 10 days.
 City Cast DC asked Bowser for comment on Tuesday morning. Her office has not yet responded.
 The provision on who can take office hasn’t come up because it’s been decades since the District has had a new delegate. Holmes Norton, the current delegate, has been in the role since 1991 and was previously the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and a professor at Georgetown University. Her predecessor, Walter Fauntroy, was a pastor when he was elected.
 The D.C. Delegate is a member of Congress who fights for D.C. statehood on the Hill and serves on committees but is not allowed to cast votes on final pieces of legislation.
 As the Democratic nominee, White is all but guaranteed to win the election next week.
 If he resigns, that would further muddy the process to replace him. The D.C. Democratic State Committee over the summer considered a proposal to hold a massive, 1,200-person party convention to pick White’s replacement. They want to avoid what happened in 2012 when the 71-member committee voted to place Anita Bonds into the at-large council seat left vacant when Phil Mendelson ascended to Council chair.
 Phil Pannell, Ward 8 activist and party national committeeman, told the 51st over the summer that he was inspired by Maine Democrats holding a large convention to replace their nominee after Graham Platner dropped out of the U.S. Senate race.
 According to D.C. code , the party — using its own process — will put somebody in the role until an election can be held at least 70 days but no more than 174 after the vacancy in a contest run by the D.C. Board of Elections.
 White is shepherding multiple bills on the housing committee that would make housing more equitable, including proposals that would speed up the resolution of eviction cases and adjust how the city distributes funds for affordable developments. Some in the Wilson Building fear that his proposals would fall by the wayside if the housing committee was left without a chair so soon before the legislative period ends.
 Staff for Mendelson told City Cast DC on Tuesday that the Council chair is asking councilmembers if they want any bills moved from the housing committee to his committee so they can still have a chance of passing.
 Ben Brasch 
 Politics & Government Reporter Ben Brasch is the politics and government reporter for City Cast DC.
